mainTopic: End of the משנה on extending a city's תחום שבת (bridges, monuments, squaring the city), then the גמרא's opening dispute between רב and שמואל on the wording מעברין or מאברין, followed by a related dispute about the shape of מערת המכפלה.
overview: This amud finishes the משנה about measuring a city's תחום שבת. Bridges and monuments that contain a living space extend the city's edge, and the whole city is then treated as a square so it gains the corners. The גמרא opens with a dispute between רב and שמואל: is the משנה's word מעברין (like a pregnant woman's belly) or מאברין (adding limbs)? It then brings a chain of other רב and שמואל disputes: the shape of מערת המכפלה, whether אמרפל or נמרוד was the real name, and whether the 'new king' of מצרים was truly new. Next, רבי יוחנן reports that in eighteen days with רבי אושעיא he learned only that מאברין is spelled with an א. The גמרא challenges this from his other statement that he learned the heart and wisdom of each student there, and reconciles the two in three different ways. This leads to praise of great teachers and to sayings about how each generation's understanding, reasoning and memory have weakened. The amud ends with explanations of why Torah lasted in יהודה but not in the גליל: precise language and סימנים, learning from one teacher, and announcing the מסכתא in advance. That last point is illustrated by דוד and שאול, and the פסוק about שאול continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Bridges and monuments with a residence extend the city's border
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that bridges and grave monuments that contain a living space count as part of the city, so the city's outline is extended opposite them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Bridges and grave monuments that have a living space in them: we extend the city's measurement out to match them.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה is finishing its list of structures that count as part of the city when we measure its תחום שבת. It adds bridges and monuments, but only if someone could live in them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a bridge or a monument over a grave is not a home, so it would not stretch the city's border. The condition 'שיש בהן בית דירה' is the key: once there is a livable room, it counts like a house. The city's edge is then pushed out along that whole side, as if there were buildings there too.

keyTerms.meaning: A living space, a room fit to live in
We extend the measurement (of the city's edge)
Opposite them, in line with them

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think every bridge or monument extends the city. Only ones with a בית דירה count.

phrases.english: And bridges and monuments (over graves)
phrases.notes: Continues the list from the previous part of the משנה.

phrases.english: that have a living space in them
phrases.notes: This condition is what makes them count.

phrases.english: one extends the measurement opposite them.
phrases.notes: The city's edge is stretched out to line up with them.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּגְשָׁרִים וּנְפָשׁוֹת שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהֶן בֵּית דִּירָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list (begun on the previous daf) of protrusions that extend a city's border.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bridges and monuments containing a residence extend the city's measured border opposite them.

steps.title: The city is squared off so it gains the corners
steps.stepSummary: Before measuring the תחום, the city is treated as a perfect square tablet, so empty corners are counted as part of the city.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we make the city like a square tablet, so that it gains the corners.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a final measuring rule. Whatever shape the city really has, we draw a square around it before measuring the 2,000 אמות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A city may be round or uneven, leaving empty corners with no houses. The משנה says to fill them in anyway by drawing a square around the city. This helps the residents, because the 2,000 אמות are measured from the corners of that bigger square.

keyTerms.meaning: A square tablet; a square shape

steps.whatToRemember: End of the משנה: livable protrusions extend the city's edge, and then the whole city is squared off so it gains the corners.
steps.whyThisMatters: This squaring principle is a basic tool for measuring any city's תחום שבת. It always works in the residents' favor.

phrases.english: And one makes it (the city) like a kind of square tablet,
so that it gains the corners.
phrases.notes: Even corners with no houses are counted.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעוֹשִׂין אוֹתָהּ כְּמִין טַבְלָא מְרוּבַּעַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the final step of the measuring process after the protrusions have been included.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The city is treated as a square before measuring, so it gains the corners.

steps.title: רב and שמואל disagree on how to spell the משנה's key word
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens with a disagreement between רב and שמואל: one reads the משנה's word as מעברין (with an ע׳), the other as מאברין (with an א׳).
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רב and שמואל: one taught 'מעברין' and one taught 'מאברין'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by looking at the משנה's opening word, 'כיצד מעברין את הערים'. It reports that רב and שמואל read that word differently, and it is setting up an explanation of each reading in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two words sound almost the same but are spelled with different letters, ע׳ and א׳. The גמרא does not yet tell us what each spelling means. That comes next. The two readings do not change the law; each one gives a different picture of how a city is expanded.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmudic discussion on the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: The word being argued about is from the beginning of the משנה (כיצד מעברין את הערים), not from the lines about bridges and corners just above.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Rav and Shmuel (disagreed):
phrases.notes: The two great early אמוראים of Babylonia.

phrases.english: one taught 'me'abberin' (with an ayin)
and one taught 'me'abberin' (with an alef).
phrases.notes: The גמרא does not say which one held which reading.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל: חַד תָּנֵי ״מְעַבְּרִין״ וְחַד תָּנֵי ״מְאַבְּרִין״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the משנה to a discussion of the משנה's opening word.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are two readings of the משנה's verb: מעברין and מאברין.

steps.title: What each reading means: limbs or a pregnant belly
steps.stepSummary: מאברין comes from אבר (a limb): the city gets limbs added to it. מעברין comes from עוברה (a pregnant woman): the city's protrusions are like a pregnant belly that sticks out.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who taught 'מאברין' means limb by limb. The one who taught 'מעברין' means like a pregnant woman.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains the reason behind each spelling from the previous step. Each spelling gives a picture of how a city's border is extended.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With an א׳, the word is tied to אבר, a limb. The protruding houses are like limbs added onto the body of the city. With an ע׳, the word is tied to a pregnant woman, whose belly sticks out but is still part of her. In the same way, the city's protrusions are part of the city.
steps.whatToRemember: Both readings describe the same law. The city's protrusions count as part of it, pictured either as added limbs (א׳) or as a pregnant belly (ע׳).

phrases.english: The one who taught 'me'abberin' (with an alef):
(it means) limb by limb,
phrases.notes: Parts are added onto the city like limbs.

phrases.english: and the one who taught 'me'abberin' (with an ayin):
(it means) like a pregnant woman.
phrases.notes: Her belly sticks out but is still part of her.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּתָנֵי ״מְאַבְּרִין״ — אֵבֶר אֵבֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the meaning behind each of the two readings in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מאברין means adding limbs; מעברין means protruding like a pregnant belly.

steps.title: רב and שמואל disagree about the layout of מערת המכפלה
steps.stepSummary: Since the גמרא just quoted a רב and שמואל dispute, it brings another one. Was מערת המכפלה two rooms, one behind the other, or a room with a second story above it?
steps.simpleTranslation: מערת המכפלה: רב and שמואל disagree. One said: two rooms, one farther in than the other. The other said: a room and an upper story above it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a side topic. It brings another dispute between רב and שמואל, this time about the shape of the cave where the אבות and אמהות are buried.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This step is not connected to תחום שבת. It is brought because it is another case where רב and שמואל argue, with 'חד אמר … וחד אמר', and we are not told who said what. One view sees the 'doubling' as two rooms side by side, one deeper inside. The other sees it as two levels, one on top of the other.

keyTerms.meaning: The cave of מכפלה, burial place of the אבות and אמהות
One farther inside than the other

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new law about תחום שבת. The גמרא is collecting similar רב and שמואל disputes.

phrases.english: The Machpelah Cave,
phrases.notes: New topic, brought because it is another רב and שמואל dispute.

phrases.english: Rav and Shmuel (disagreed):
One said: two rooms,
one farther in than the other,
phrases.notes: Side by side, going deeper.

phrases.english: and one said: a room
and an upper story on top of it.
phrases.notes: Stacked one above the other.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְעָרַת הַמַּכְפֵּלָה, רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Linked by association: another dispute between רב and שמואל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One view: the cave was two rooms, one behind the other. Other view: a room with an upper story.

steps.title: How does the two-rooms opinion explain the name 'מכפלה'?
steps.stepSummary: The name מכפלה (double) fits the opinion that one room sits on top of the other. But according to the opinion that it was two rooms side by side, why call it 'double'?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for the one who says one room was above the other, because that is why it is called 'מכפלה' (double). But according to the one who says it was two rooms, one behind the other, why is it called 'מכפלה'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the 'two rooms, one behind the other' opinion. It asks how that opinion explains the name 'מכפלה'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A room with a second story above it is truly 'doubled', so the name fits that view well. Plenty of ordinary houses have an inner room and an outer room, so the name seems to add nothing for the side-by-side view. The question is aimed only at the side-by-side opinion.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense / granted (opens a question that works for one side but not the other)
מכפלה, from the word for 'double' or 'folded'
One on top of the other
One further inside than the other

phrases.aramaic: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר זֶה עַל גַּב זֶה —
phrases.english: Granted, according to the one who said one above the other —
that is why it is called 'Machpelah' (double).
But according to the one who said
two rooms, one further in than the other,
in what sense is it 'Machpelah'?
phrases.notes: Every house has an inner and outer room, so what is 'double' about it?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר זֶה עַל גַּב זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the two opinions from Step 5 against the name of the cave.
steps.kashyaTarget: The opinion that מערת המכפלה was two rooms, one behind the other
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The name 'double' only fits a cave that is stacked. A side-by-side layout is ordinary and does not explain the name.

steps.title: It is 'doubled' with couples
steps.stepSummary: The name מכפלה refers to the couples buried there, not to the shape of the cave.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is called that because it is doubled with pairs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for the side-by-side opinion. The cave is called 'double' because couples (husband and wife) are buried there in pairs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer moves the meaning of 'double' from the building to the people buried inside. This way the side-by-side opinion no longer needs the shape of the cave to explain the name.

phrases.english: Because it is doubled with pairs.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁכְּפוּלָה בְּזוּגוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 6.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Double' had to describe the cave's structure.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Double' describes the couples buried in the cave, so the side-by-side opinion stands.

steps.title: קרית ארבע means the city of four couples
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק explains that קרית ארבע, the city of מערת המכפלה, is named after the four couples buried there.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'ממרא קרית ארבע': רבי יצחק said, it is the city of the four couples: אדם and חוה, אברהם and שרה, יצחק and רבקה, יעקב and לאה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבי יצחק's teaching as a parallel to the answer in Step 7. The city's own name, 'city of four', also points to the couples buried there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 said the cave is named for couples. Here the city חברון is also named for those same couples, so the idea of naming the place after its buried pairs is not new. It also tells us who the couples are.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The city of four', another name for חברון

steps.whatToRemember: According to the 'two rooms' opinion, מכפלה means 'doubled with couples'. The four couples are אדם and חוה, אברהם and שרה, יצחק and רבקה, and יעקב and לאה.

phrases.english: 'Mamre, Kiryat Arba' (Bereishis 35:27),
Rabbi Yitzchak said,
the city of the four couples:
Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah,
Isaac and Rebecca, Jacob and Leah.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַמְרֵא קִרְיַת אַרְבַּע אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a parallel teaching that backs up the 'couples' explanation of Step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קרית ארבע is named after the four couples buried there.

steps.title: Who was Amraphel?
steps.stepSummary: Another רב and שמואל dispute: both agree that אמרפל and נמרוד are the same person, but they argue about which name is his real name.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And it was in the days of אמרפל': רב and שמואל. One said his name was נמרוד. Why was he called אמרפל? Because he said the order and threw אברהם אבינו into the fiery furnace. The other said his name was אמרפל. Why was he called נמרוד? Because he made the whole world rebel against ה׳ during his rule.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues its list of רב and שמואל disputes. They argue about whether נמרוד or אמרפל was his real name, and each side explains the other name as a nickname.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that it is one person. If נמרוד is the real name, then אמרפל comes from 'אמר' (said) plus 'הפיל' (threw), describing how he ordered אברהם thrown into the furnace. If אמרפל is the real name, then נמרוד comes from 'המריד' (caused to rebel), because he led the world in rebellion against ה׳.

keyTerms.meaning: A king in בראשית 14, read as 'אָמַר וְהִפִּיל' (said and threw)
Read as coming from 'הִמְרִיד' (caused to rebel)
One said (used when we don't know which רבי said which view)

steps.confusionAlert: They do NOT argue about whether אמרפל and נמרוד are two different people. Both agree they are the same person. The only question is which name is the real one and which is the nickname.

phrases.english: 'And it was in the days of Amraphel' (Bereishis 14:1),
Rav and Shmuel disagree,
one said: Nimrod was his name.
And why was he called Amraphel?
Because he said (amar) and cast (hippil) our father Abraham
into the fiery furnace,
and one said: Amraphel was his name,
and why was he called Nimrod?
Because he caused the entire world to rebel (himrid)
against Him (ה׳) during his reign.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיְהִי בִּימֵי אַמְרָפֶל רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another dispute to the list of רב and שמואל disagreements that began in Step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אמרפל and נמרוד are one person. They argue only about which name is primary and how the other name is explained.

steps.title: Was the new king of Egypt really new?
steps.stepSummary: A final רב and שמואל dispute: was the 'new king' of מצרים a truly new king, or the same king with new decrees?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And a new king arose over מצרים': רב and שמואל. One said he was truly new. The other said his decrees became new.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more רב and שמואל dispute. They argue about how to read the words 'new king' in שמות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One opinion reads the פסוק literally: a different person became king. The other says it was the same old king, and he is called 'new' because he started making new, harsh decrees against the Jews.
steps.whatToRemember: This section is a chain of רב and שמואל disputes: מעברין or מאברין, the shape of מערת המכפלה, אמרפל and נמרוד, and the 'new king' of מצרים.

phrases.english: 'And a new king arose over Egypt' (Shemos 1:8),
Rav and Shmuel disagree,
one said: actually new,
and one said: that his decrees were renewed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיָּקׇם מֶלֶךְ חָדָשׁ עַל מִצְרָיִם רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of רב and שמואל disputes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One view says it was a different king. The other says it was the same king with new decrees.

steps.title: The verse-based source for each opinion about the new king
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows which part of the פסוק supports each side. One side relies on the word חדש (new). The other relies on the missing phrase 'and he died and he reigned.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who says he was truly a new king relies on the פסוק calling him 'new.' The one who says only his decrees were new relies on the fact that the פסוק does not say 'and [the old king] died, and [a new one] reigned.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the source in the פסוק for each of the two opinions from the previous step about the 'new king.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion reads the word חדש literally: a new person took the throne. The second opinion points to what is missing. When the תורה reports a true change of kings, as with the kings of אדום, it says 'he died and another reigned.' Here it does not say that, so it must be the same king acting in a new way.

keyTerms.meaning: Truly new: an actual new king
His decrees became new: the same king with new policies
'And he died, and he reigned': the phrase the תורה uses for a change of kings
From the fact that it is not written

phrases.english: The one who said he was actually new —
because it is written 'new,'
phrases.notes: He reads the word at face value.

phrases.english: and the one who said that his decrees were made new —
[learns it] from the fact that it is not written 'and he died, and he reigned.'
phrases.notes: Compare the list of the kings of אדום in בראשית ל״ו, which uses this phrasing.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּאָמַר חָדָשׁ מַמָּשׁ דִּכְתִיב חָדָשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the textual basis for each side of the dispute presented in step 10.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The word חדש in the פסוק, and the absence of the phrase וימת וימלוך

steps.title: Challenge: how could the same king not know יוסף?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the 'new decrees' opinion. The פסוק says the king 'did not know יוסף,' and that seems impossible if he was the same king.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who says only his decrees were new, the פסוק says 'who did not know יוסף.' How can that be?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the second opinion using the next words in the same פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If this was the same פרעה who raised יוסף to power, he obviously knew יוסף. So the words 'who did not know יוסף' seem to prove that this was a different person, which supports the first opinion.

keyTerms.meaning: And according to the one who said
But it is written: the standard opening of a challenge from a פסוק

phrases.english: And according to the one who said that his decrees were made new,

phrases.aramaic: הָא כְתִיב ״אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָדַע אֶת יוֹסֵף״?
phrases.english: isn't it written 'who did not know Joseph'?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר שֶׁנִּתְחַדְּשׁוּ גְּזֵירוֹתָיו הָא כְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the second opinion whose source was just given.
steps.kashyaTarget: The opinion that it was the same king with new decrees
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same king would certainly have known יוסף, yet the פסוק says he did not.

steps.title: He acted as if he never knew יוסף
steps.stepSummary: 'Did not know יוסף' describes how the king behaved. It does not mean he had no knowledge of him.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'who did not know יוסף' mean? That he acted like someone who did not know יוסף at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by reading 'did not know' as a description of behavior.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The king knew יוסף perfectly well, but he ignored everything יוסף had done for מצרים. He treated יוסף's people as though יוסף had never existed. So the 'new decrees' opinion stands.
steps.whatToRemember: Both opinions about the 'new king' survive. One reads חדש literally. The other says it was the same פרעה, who acted as if he never knew יוסף.

phrases.english: What is [the meaning of] 'who did not know Joseph'? —
that he was like someone
who did not know Joseph at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָדַע אֶת יוֹסֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the פסוק's wording: from not knowing to acting as if he did not know
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Did not know יוסף' means a different king who never met him.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means the same king ignored יוסף completely.

steps.title: A memory aid for the teachings that follow
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a סימן, a string of key words that will help the learner remember the order of the upcoming teachings.
steps.simpleTranslation: (A memory aid: eighteen and twelve, we learned, about דוד, and he will understand.)
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. It is not an argument. It lists one key word from each of the coming statements so the learner can remember them in order.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Eighteen' points to the very next statement, where רבי יוחנן spent eighteen days with רבי אושעיא. The other words point to teachings that come later on the דף. Nothing is proven or argued here.

keyTerms.meaning: A memory aid that strings together key words from upcoming teachings
'And he will understand': a key word pointing to a later teaching

steps.confusionAlert: Do not try to find a meaning or argument in this line. It is only a list of reminder words, like a table of contents.

phrases.english: (A mnemonic:
eighteen and twelve,
we learned, with David, and he will understand.)

steps.triggerLanguage: סִימָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Marks the end of the רב and שמואל section and previews a new series of teachings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling. This is a structural memory aid for the upcoming statements.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן's one lesson from רבי אושעיא: מאברין is spelled with an א
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says he spent eighteen days with רבי אושעיא בריבי. He learned only one point from him: in our משנה, the word מאברין is spelled with an א.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: I spent eighteen days with רבי אושעיא בריבי, and I learned from him only one thing in our משנה. In the line 'How does one extend the cities?', the word מאברין is spelled with an א.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רבי יוחנן reports the single detail he picked up from his short time with רבי אושעיא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה (עירובין 52b) speaks about extending a city's borders for measuring the תחום שבת. רב and שמואל already argued (steps 3–4) whether the word is מאברין with an א (limb by limb) or מעברין with an ע (like a pregnant woman). רבי אושעיא's tradition backs the א reading. The next step questions whether רבי יוחנן really learned only this one point.

keyTerms.meaning: I spent time with (literally: I grew up with)
Extending the cities: adding to a city's outline for measuring its boundary

steps.confusionAlert: Both מאברין (with א) and מעברין (with ע) sound alike. The whole point here is the spelling, not the pronunciation.
steps.whyThisMatters: This opens a discussion about the exact wording of the משנה. It shows how much weight חז״ל placed on a single letter in a text.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
Eighteen days I spent
phrases.notes: Matches 'eighteen' in the סימן.

phrases.english: with Rabbi Oshaya the Distinguished,
and I learned from him nothing
except one matter in our Mishnah:
'How does one extend the cities' —
[the word me'abberin is spelled] with an alef.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן שְׁמוֹנָה עָשָׂר יָמִים גִּידַּלְתִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The first teaching previewed by the סימן ('eighteen').
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word מאברין in the משנה is correctly spelled with an א.

steps.title: Did רבי יוחנן really learn only one thing there?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא contrasts two statements of רבי יוחנן. One says he learned only one point. The other says he learned the heart and wisdom of every student of רבי אושעיא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רבי יוחנן said that רבי אושעיא בריבי had twelve students, and he spent eighteen days among them. He said he learned the heart and the wisdom of every single one of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question against step 15. רבי יוחנן said elsewhere that in those eighteen days he learned a lot, not just one point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 sounds like the eighteen days produced almost nothing, only the spelling of מאברין. This second statement describes a rich eighteen days in which רבי יוחנן came to know each student's character and wisdom. The two statements seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? An opening word for a challenge
I spent time among them, literally 'I grew among them'
Heart, meaning a person's nature and character
Wisdom, meaning how much a person knows

phrases.english: Is that so?! But didn't Rabbi Yochanan say:
Twelve students he had
Rabbi Oshaya the Distinguished,
and eighteen days I spent among them,
phrases.notes: These are the same eighteen days mentioned in step 15.

phrases.english: and I learned the heart of each and every one,
and the wisdom of each and every one?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי?! וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claim in step 15 that רבי יוחנן learned only one point.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's statement that in eighteen days he learned only one point (מאברין with an א)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another statement of his says he learned the heart and wisdom of all twelve students in those same days, so he did not learn just one thing.

steps.title: He learned about people, not learning content
steps.stepSummary: First answer: he came to know the students' character and level, but he did not gain actual Torah content.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learned the heart and wisdom of each one, but he did not learn גמרא, meaning actual Torah tradition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its first answer to the question. The two statements talk about two different kinds of learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Getting to know who each student is, and how smart he is, is different from learning Torah material. When רבי יוחנן said he learned only one thing, he meant one thing of real content. Both statements can be true.

keyTerms.meaning: Learned tradition, the actual Torah content passed down

steps.confusionAlert: Here the word גְּמָרָא does not mean 'the book of גמרא.' It means Torah tradition that is received and studied.

phrases.english: The heart of each and every one
and the wisdom of each and every one, he learned;
tradition, he did not learn.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵב כׇּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד וְחׇכְמַת כׇּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד גְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes between two kinds of learning
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Learning' in both statements means the same thing, so they contradict.
steps.terutzMaskana: One statement is about knowing the people, and the other is about Torah content.

steps.title: From the students he learned, from the teacher only one thing
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: he learned a lot from the students. From רבי אושעיא himself he learned only one point.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you could say: from the students themselves he learned, but from רבי אושעיא himself he did not learn more.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different answer. The two statements are about two different sources: the students and the teacher.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'one point' statement was about what came from רבי אושעיא directly. The 'learned the heart and wisdom' statement was about what he gained from the twelve students. So the two statements do not clash.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say this instead. It introduces another answer

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
from the students themselves, he learned;
from Rabbi Oshaya himself, he did not learn.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: מִנַּיְיהוּ דִּידְהוּ גְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another answer to the same question, in place of step 17.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both statements are about the same source.
steps.terutzMaskana: He learned much from the students, but only one point from the teacher.

steps.title: Only one point in our משנה
steps.stepSummary: Third answer: he learned only one point about our specific משנה, but he learned other things too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you could say: he meant that he learned only one point about our משנה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third answer. רבי יוחנן's 'only one point' was limited to our משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer reads step 15 narrowly. About this particular משנה he picked up only the spelling of מאברין. In other areas, such as ברייתות, he learned much more, so nothing contradicts.

keyTerms.meaning: He is saying, meaning this is what he meant

steps.whatToRemember: There are three ways to fit the two statements together. (1) He learned about the people, not Torah content. (2) He learned from the students, not from the teacher. (3) He learned only one point about our משנה.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
he meant one matter in our Mishnah.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: דָּבָר אֶחָד בְּמִשְׁנָתֵינוּ קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to the question in step 16. It closes that discussion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of the original statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Only one point' meant one point in everything he learned.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Only one point' was limited to our משנה.

steps.title: Four students crowded into each אמה at רבי אושעיא's
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן describes how packed רבי אושעיא's study hall was.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: When we learned Torah with רבי אושעיא, we sat four to each אמה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another statement of רבי יוחנן about learning with רבי אושעיא. It shows how many students came to learn from him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sitting four students in a single square אמה is extremely crowded. The point is how popular רבי אושעיא was and how much students wanted to hear him.

keyTerms.meaning: A cubit, about half a meter. Here it means a square אמה of space

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
When we were studying Torah
with Rabbi Oshaya,
we would sit four in each cubit.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: כְּשֶׁהָיִינוּ לוֹמְדִין תּוֹרָה אֵצֶל רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another memory of רבי יוחנן about רבי אושעיא's study hall.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אושעיא's study hall was so full that four students sat in each square אמה.

steps.title: Six students in each אמה at רבי אלעזר בן שמוע's
steps.stepSummary: רבי makes a similar statement about the crowding in the study hall of רבי אלעזר בן שמוע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי said: When we learned Torah with רבי אלעזר בן שמוע, we sat six to each אמה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a statement that matches the last one. רבי tells about an even more crowded study hall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This uses the same wording as רבי יוחנן's statement, but with six students instead of four. It shows an even bigger crowd around רבי אלעזר בן שמוע.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said:
When we were studying Torah
with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua,
we would sit six in each cubit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי: כְּשֶׁהָיִינוּ לוֹמְדִין תּוֹרָה אֵצֶל רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן שַׁמּוּעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A matching statement about a different teacher, with even more crowding.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אלעזר בן שמוע's study hall was so crowded that six students sat in each square אמה.

steps.title: רבי אושעיא was like רבי מאיר in his generation
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that, like רבי מאיר, רבי אושעיא was so deep that his colleagues could not reach the full depth of his thinking.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: רבי אושעיא בריבי in his generation was like רבי מאיר in his generation. רבי מאיר's colleagues could not fully understand how deep his thinking went. In the same way, רבי אושעיא's colleagues could not fully understand how deep his thinking went.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן praises his teacher. He compares רבי אושעיא to רבי מאיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר was known as so sharp that his peers could not follow his reasoning all the way to the end. By using the same comparison, רבי יוחנן puts רבי אושעיא at that level of genius.

keyTerms.meaning: To reach the full depth of his thinking
Just as... so too. A comparison pattern

steps.whatToRemember: רבי אושעיא בריבי was a towering scholar. He drew crowds of students, and like רבי מאיר, his colleagues could not grasp the full depth of his thinking.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
Rabbi Oshaya the Distinguished, in his generation,
was like Rabbi Meir in his generation:
just as with Rabbi Meir, in his generation
his colleagues were unable
to fully grasp the depth of his thinking,
so too Rabbi Oshaya:
his colleagues were unable
to fully grasp the depth of his thinking.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא בְּרִיבִּי בְּדוֹרוֹ כְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר בְּדוֹרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues praising רבי אושעיא, moving from the size of his crowd to the depth of his mind.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אושעיא was as great as רבי מאיר. His colleagues could not reach the full depth of his thinking.

steps.title: The minds of earlier and later sages compared to doorways in the Temple
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the minds of the earliest sages were as wide as the doorway of the אולם. The later sages' minds were like the smaller doorway of the היכל. Our minds are like the eye of a fine needle.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: The hearts of the early sages were like the doorway of the אולם, and the hearts of the later sages were like the doorway of the היכל. And we are like the full hole of a fine needle.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a picture to show how much smaller each generation's understanding has become.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The doorway of the אולם was 20 אמות wide and 40 high. The doorway of the היכל was half that size, 10 by 20. So each step is a big drop, and our generation is tiny by comparison, like the eye of a needle.

keyTerms.meaning: Their hearts, meaning their minds and understanding
The entrance hall of the בית המקדש, which had a very large doorway
The Sanctuary inside the אולם, which had a smaller doorway
A fine needle, used for delicate sewing

steps.confusionAlert: In this context, 'heart' (לב) means the mind and the capacity to understand. It does not mean feelings.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: לִבָּן שֶׁל רִאשׁוֹנִים כְּפִתְחוֹ שֶׁל אוּלָם,
phrases.english: The hearts of the early ones were like the doorway of the Entrance Hall,
phrases.notes: That doorway was 20 by 40 אמות.

phrases.english: and those of the later ones were like the doorway of the Sanctuary,
phrases.notes: That doorway was 10 by 20 אמות, half the size.

phrases.english: and we are like the full eye of a fine needle.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: לִבָּן שֶׁל רִאשׁוֹנִים כְּפִתְחוֹ שֶׁל אוּלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the praise of רבי אושעיא and other great sages with a broader statement about how the generations have declined.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Understanding has shrunk greatly from generation to generation: from the size of the אולם doorway, to the היכל doorway, to the eye of a needle.

steps.title: Identifying the earlier and later sages: first version
steps.stepSummary: The 'early' sages are רבי עקיבא, and the 'later' sages are his student רבי אלעזר בן שמוע.
steps.simpleTranslation: The early ones are רבי עקיבא. The later ones are רבי אלעזר בן שמוע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains who רבי יוחנן meant by 'early' and 'later' sages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This turns the general picture into specific people. רבי עקיבא is the huge אולם doorway, and his student רבי אלעזר בן שמוע is the smaller היכל doorway. This fits the earlier praise of רבי אלעזר בן שמוע's crowded study hall.

phrases.english: The early ones means Rabbi Akiva;
the later ones means Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua.

steps.triggerLanguage: רִאשׁוֹנִים — רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the terms ראשונים and אחרונים from רבי יוחנן's statement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ראשונים refers to רבי עקיבא, and אחרונים refers to רבי אלעזר בן שמוע.

steps.title: Identifying the earlier and later sages: second version
steps.stepSummary: Some say the 'early' sage is רבי אלעזר בן שמוע and the 'later' sage is רבי אושעיא בריבי. Either way, we are like the eye of a fine needle.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: The early ones are רבי אלעזר בן שמוע, and the later ones are רבי אושעיא בריבי. And we are like the full eye of a fine needle.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of who the early and later sages are.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version everyone moves one generation down. רבי אלעזר בן שמוע becomes the 'early' sage, and רבי אושעיא, whose study hall was just praised, becomes the 'later' sage. The ending stays the same: our minds are like the eye of a needle.

phrases.english: Some say:
The early ones means Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua;
the later ones means Rabbi Oshaya the Distinguished.
And we are like the full eye of a fine needle.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: רִאשׁוֹנִים — רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן שַׁמּוּעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different identification from step 24.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ראשונים refers to רבי אלעזר בן שמוע, and אחרונים refers to רבי אושעיא בריבי.

steps.title: אביי: we are like a peg going into a wall when we learn
steps.stepSummary: אביי says that in learning, we are like a peg pushed into a wall: the knowledge goes in only with great difficulty.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: And we, in learning, are like a peg in a wall.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי adds his own picture of his generation's weakness, focusing on taking in what we learn.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A peg goes into a wall only with hard pushing. In the same way, learning goes into our minds only with great effort. אביי's point is about absorbing the material, which is what גמרא means here.

keyTerms.meaning: Here: learning and absorbing what one is taught

phrases.english: Abaye said:
And we are like a peg in a wall with regard to learning.
phrases.notes: The peg goes in only with difficulty.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: וַאֲנַן, כִּי סִיכְּתָא בְּגוּדָּא לִגְמָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of decline with a new picture from a later אמורא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Our generation takes in learning only with great difficulty.

steps.title: רבא: we are like a finger pushed into wax when we reason
steps.stepSummary: רבא says that in reasoning, we are like a finger pushed into wax: it is hard to go deep, and little comes out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: And we, in logical reasoning, are like a finger in wax.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second picture of weakness, this time about understanding through reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי spoke about absorbing what we learn. רבא speaks about working out new understanding. A finger pushes into wax only with difficulty and does not bring anything out, just as our reasoning goes deep only with effort.

phrases.english: Rava said:
And we are like a finger in wax with regard to reasoning.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: וַאֲנַן, כִּי אֶצְבַּעְתָּא בְּקִירָא לִסְבָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel to אביי's statement but about a different skill: reasoning instead of absorbing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Our generation's reasoning goes deep only with great difficulty.

steps.title: רב אשי: we are like a finger in a pit when it comes to forgetting
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says that in forgetting, we are like a finger going into a pit: it goes in easily, meaning we forget quickly.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: We, in forgetting, are like a finger in a pit.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי finishes the series of three pictures with one about memory.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first two pictures showed how hard things are to get in. This one flips the image: a finger slips into a wide pit with no effort, and in the same way our learning slips away easily. Together the three cover learning, reasoning, and remembering.
steps.whatToRemember: Three אמוראים, three pictures: אביי (peg in a wall) is about absorbing learning, רבא (finger in wax) is about reasoning, and רב אשי (finger in a pit) is about how easily we forget.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
We are like a finger in a pit with regard to forgetting.
phrases.notes: It goes in easily, so we forget easily.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: אֲנַן, כִּי אֶצְבַּעְתָּא בְּבֵירָא לְשִׁכְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the series of three pictures, now focused on memory.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Our generation forgets its learning very easily.

steps.title: People of Judea kept their Torah because they were careful in speech; people of the Galilee did not
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב says the people of יהודה were careful and precise in their speech, so their Torah stayed with them. The people of the גליל were not careful, so their Torah did not stay with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: The people of יהודה, who were careful about their speech, kept their Torah. The people of the גליל, who were not careful about their speech, did not keep their Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new teaching about what helps Torah learning last: being careful and precise in how one speaks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After describing weak memory, the גמרא now gives a cause for keeping Torah: being careful in speech. The next step immediately questions whether 'being particular' alone could really be the cause, and then re-explains the statement in practical terms.

keyTerms.meaning: The Galilee, the northern region of ארץ ישראל

steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches that clear, exact speech is not a small detail. It is connected to remembering and keeping one's Torah.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
The people of Judea, who were particular about their speech,
their Torah endured in their hands.

phrases.aramaic: בְּנֵי גָלִיל שֶׁלֹּא הִקְפִּידוּ עַל לְשׁוֹנָם,
phrases.english: The people of the Galilee, who were not particular about their speech,
their Torah did not endure in their hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: בְּנֵי יְהוּדָה שֶׁהִקְפִּידוּ עַל לְשׁוֹנָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from describing weak memory to naming something that helps Torah last.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Being careful and precise in speech helps one's Torah endure; being careless with speech causes it to be lost.

steps.title: Does It Really Depend on Being Careful?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the explanation from Step 29. Can keeping one's Torah really depend on just being 'careful' (קפידא)?
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this matter really depend on being particular?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions רב's statement from Step 29. It asks whether keeping Torah could really depend on simply being 'particular.' This question sets up a better explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taken at face value, רב's words suggest that a general attitude of being particular is what made Torah last. The גמרא finds that strange, since an attitude alone should not decide whether learning stays with a person. So it pushes for a more concrete explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it at all? (a word that opens a doubtful or challenging question)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a brand-new topic. The גמרא is questioning the wording of רב's statement from Step 29, so it can explain that statement more precisely.

phrases.english: Does the matter at all depend on being particular?
phrases.notes: A challenge phrased as a question; it expects the answer 'no.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מִידֵּי בִּקְפֵידָא תַּלְיָא מִילְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how Step 29 was worded.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that Torah lasted in יהודה because they were 'careful.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being particular is only a general attitude. It is hard to see how it alone could decide whether learning is remembered.

steps.title: Precise Wording and Memory Aids
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא re-explains רב's statement. The people of יהודה used exact wording and made up סימנים (memory aids), so their Torah stayed with them. The people of the גליל did neither, so it did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: the people of יהודה, who were precise in their language and made memory aids for themselves, kept their Torah. The people of the גליל, who were not precise in their language and did not make memory aids, did not keep their Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question. It explains that 'careful' really means two practical habits: speaking precisely and making סימנים to remember what they learned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The vague idea of 'being particular' is replaced with two concrete learning tools. Exact wording keeps the material clear, and סימנים help a person recall it. These tools, not an attitude, are why the learning lasted.

keyTerms.meaning: they are precise in their language
they set up memory aids for themselves
their Torah stayed with them (they remembered their learning)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a source for the long-standing practice of using סימנים in learning. The גמרא itself uses them often.

phrases.english: Rather: the people of Judea, who were precise in their language,
and would set up memory aids for themselves,
their Torah endured in their hands.
The people of the Galilee, who were not precise in their language,
and would not set up memory aids for themselves,
their Torah did not endure in their hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: בְּנֵי יְהוּדָה דְּדָיְיקִי לִישָּׁנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 30 by restating רב's idea in practical terms.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Torah lasted because of a general attitude of being particular.
steps.terutzMaskana: Torah lasted because of precise language and the use of סימנים.

steps.title: Learning From One Teacher
steps.stepSummary: A second reason: the people of יהודה learned from one teacher (חד רבה), so their Torah lasted. The people of the גליל learned from many teachers, so it did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: The people of יהודה learned from one teacher, and their Torah stayed with them. The people of the גליל, who did not learn from one teacher, did not keep their Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another reason why Torah lasted in יהודה: they learned from a single teacher.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One teacher gives a student one consistent style and way of explaining things. Learning from many teachers mixes different approaches, which makes the material harder to keep straight and remember.

phrases.english: The people of Judea learned from one teacher,
so their Torah endured in their hands.

phrases.aramaic: בְּנֵי גָלִיל דְּלָא גָּמְרִי מֵחַד רַבָּה,
phrases.english: The people of the Galilee, who did not learn from one teacher,
their Torah did not endure in their hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּנֵי יְהוּדָה גְּמַרוּ מֵחַד רַבָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, separate reason alongside Step 31.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Learning from a single teacher helps Torah last.

steps.title: רבינא: Announcing the מסכתא Ahead of Time
steps.stepSummary: רבינא gives a third reason. In יהודה they announced the upcoming מסכתא, so everyone could prepare, and their Torah lasted. In the גליל they did not, and it did not last.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: the people of יהודה, who made the tractate known, kept their Torah. The people of the גליל, who did not make the tractate known, did not keep their Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא offers his own explanation. The key difference was publicly announcing which מסכתא would be learned next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When students know the upcoming מסכתא, they can review and prepare it in advance. They then come to the שיעור ready and absorb it more deeply. Without the announcement, the learning catches them unprepared.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
The people of Judea, who disclosed the tractate,
their Torah endured in their hands.
The people of the Galilee, who did not disclose the tractate,
their Torah did not endure in their hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבִינָא אָמַר: בְּנֵי יְהוּדָה דְּגַלּוֹ מַסֶּכְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third explanation of רב's statement, given by רבינא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Announcing the מסכתא in advance helps Torah last.

steps.title: דוד and שאול as an Example
steps.stepSummary: דוד announced the מסכתא and שאול did not. For each one, a פסוק is brought that describes him. This passage ends in the middle of the פסוק about שאול.
steps.simpleTranslation: דוד would announce the tractate; שאול would not announce the tractate. About דוד, who announced the tractate, it is written: 'Those who fear You will see me and be glad.' About שאול, who did not announce the tractate, it is written: 'wherever he turned...'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports רבינא's idea with an example from two kings. דוד announced the מסכתא and שאול did not, and the פסוקים show how each one turned out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: About דוד the פסוק says that God-fearing people saw him and were happy, because they had prepared and could enjoy his Torah. The פסוק about שאול (שמואל א י״ד:מ״ז, which continues on the next amud) describes a less positive result. So the practice of announcing the מסכתא is shown to bring good results.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who fear You will see me and be glad (תהלים קי״ט:ע״ד)

steps.whatToRemember: There are three explanations for why Torah lasted in יהודה: precise language with סימנים, learning from one teacher, and announcing the מסכתא in advance. The third is backed up by the example of דוד and שאול.
